body.heading: Small fairness is real fairness
paragraphs: Children — and, honestly, adults — judge a household’s justice by its small distributions: who gets the window seat, whose turn chooses the film, who always ends up with the cracked mug. These are not trivial. They are the daily data from which people conclude whether they matter equally.
Rotas feel unglamorous, but a rota is just fairness with a memory, and it ends a hundred small negotiations before they start.

body.heading: Let people yield on purpose
paragraphs: There is a difference between always losing and sometimes giving. Teach and practise the deliberate yield: “You take the good chair tonight; I had it yesterday.” Given freely, the same chair teaches generosity instead of resentment.
Notice and name it when it happens, lightly: “Generous.” One word of recognition makes the next yield easier.

body.heading: The last slice rule
paragraphs: Many families keep a version of this rule: the person who cuts does not choose first. It is thousands of years old, works on cake, screen time, and the front seat, and children grasp its fairness instantly because it aligns interest with honesty.
Homes do not need perfect equality. They need visible fairness — systems everyone can see working, even when the outcome is not theirs.

takeaway: Build fairness into rotas and rules everyone can see, and honour the deliberate yield.
